content.comment: The authors try to stabilize the DARTS algorithm by the one-level optimization instead of the bi-level one. However, one-level optimization is not a novel idea, Single-Path NAS (https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.02877) also employed the one-level optimization, even the original DARTS paper has already tested the one-level optimization. Moreover, Single-Path NAS propose the superkernel which also combines convolutions but in a more efficient way and saves large amount of memory. I suggest the authors to read the very related work. I think the single-path models (e.g., Single Path One-Shot, Single Path NAS, FairNAS, etc.) are more  promising. Besides, there are also some important gradient-based baselines you may refer in the paper, such as XNAS, FairNAS, PCDARTS, ScarletNAS, and some of them achieve the better performance. You can get a list at https://www.automl.org/automl/literature-on-neural-architecture-search/.

display_title: We appreciate your comments. However, we respectfully disagree with your claim.

content.comment:
Hi, Andrew,
We appreciate your comments. However, we respectfully disagree with your claim.

1. You said that one-level optimization has been explored in SinglePath NAS, and thus not novel.
Please note that in the current NAS applications, the final accuracy comes from three sources: the search space;  the search method; and the final training tricks.   
 
The SinglePath NAS paper’s main point was to argue the use of a simpler one-path search space, as an alternative to multi-pass search space used by DARTS. In the simpler search space, they argued one-level optimization was good enough. There was no comparison with two-level optimization and no claim that one level optimization would work well for multi-pass space of DARTS.
 
In fact, it is not as easy to make one level optimization work well for multi-path search space of DARTS, which was already pointed out in the DARTS paper. We got one level optimization to work for the DARTS search space because we introduced the group backward search strategy and optimization complexity matching to stabilize the single-level optimization process. We believe this is highly non-trivial, and it is a significant contribution to get the simpler single-level optimization to work well with the more complex cell-based multi-path search space used by many current researchers. 
 
2. You asked for more benchmarks.
Thanks for providing the newly published related works. We'd be happy to include their results. However, these won't change the conclusion of our work. 
 
As mentioned before, in the current NAS solutions, the reported accuracies come from three sources: the search space;  the search method; and the final tricks such as data augmentation to train the model.
 
We note that the contribution of our work is to improve the search method.  Therefore we intentionally reported separately experimental results by using the same training process as that of DARTS (for a fair comparison with results in the DARTS paper), and by using additional augmentation tricks  (for a fair comparison with results in some other recent papers).
 
For other works you mentioned, such as the final architecture published by XNAS — when we tried it with the final training process used by DARTS, we could only get an accuracy of 97.4% on CIFAR-10. The reported high accuracy in their paper relies on the use of additional training tricks. Therefore when claiming one is better than the other, please take variations of final training into consideration, as we tried to make clear in our paper.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review:
This work outlined 3 problems of DARTS a) bi-level optimization, b) multicollinearity of correlated operations, c) the fundamental
challenges of matching neural network optimization complexity in NAS and in the final training. The authors proposed algorithm to fix them with a) one-level optimization b) group variable pruning and c) complexity matching by gradient confusion.

The author provided detailed experiments to support their claim of the problems of DARTS and validated their proposals with extensive benchmarks. The structure of the paper is well organized and the wording is in very good style.

I have two following minor comments:
1. Did the author do an ablation study on each of the component they proposed? For example using DARTS with only group variable pruning to highlight the contribution of it. And similarly, for one level optimization.
2. The part how to select depth using gradient confusion is not very clear to me.

content.title: The ablation study on each of the component proposed have been presented in Table 4
content.comment:
We appreciate your comments. 

 We reported the ablation studies in  Table 4 we reported the ablation studies. Results show that bi-level optimization with operation grouping and complexity matching can improve the original darts, but underperforms the proposed StacNAS. In this table, we can see how each component contributes to the final performance. 

We estimate the gradient confusion for the search stage with the stacking number of cells from  8 to 20, among which  14  matches the gradient confusion the best with the final augment stage (where 20 cells are stacked).

Please note that the optimization complexity is affected by skip-connection, width and depth. For the DARTS framework, either of those is controlled, this causes the estimation bias of the system. 

We want to take this opportunity to emphasis our contribution again, the proposed method is the first work that systematically analyzes the drawbacks of the DARTS framework, and beyond simply understanding the mechanism of it, we propose very effective solutions to solve the problems. We believe that those findings are very important to the community to better understand and use the DARTS framework.

content.review:
This paper provides a solution for stable and consistent optimization of a differentiable neural architecture search method (i.e. DARTS). Specifically, this paper introduces a grouped variable pruning algorithm based on one-level optimization and optimization complexity matching. The experimental results show that the proposed method leads to state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet datasets.

- This paper mentions that when we randomly select operations at stage 1, the final result is almost the same as that of the proposed method. How about the grouping of operations? When we randomly group the operations, how would the results change? It would be better to provide such results to clarify which parts of the proposed method contribute to the final performance.

- If possible, it would be better to compare the proposed method with recent state-of-the-art methods such as XNAS, FairNAS, PCDARTS, and ScarletNAS.

The grouping of the operations is based on whether they are correlated in a way that they would produce correlated feature maps. The estimated correlation matrix is provided in Table 5.  Identity should not be grouped with convolution because the feature maps they produced are not significantly correlated. 

Thanks for providing the relevant literature, we would add the comparison with the mentioned papers.

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Summary: 
This paper points out three major issues for the current differentiable neural architecture search (DARTS) algorithms: 1) the used bi-level optimization relies on a 2nd order approximation and thus is difficult to find the optimal solution; 2) the multicollinearity of correlated operations may not represent their real importance during architecture search; 3) the discrepancy between the complexity of the search stage architecture and the finally selected architecture. To address such three issues, the paper suggests one-level optimization with strategies of grouping similar operations in the early optimization, using a progressive pruning approach as well as a gradient confusion. 

Strength:
It is interesting that the paper studies some major drawbacks of the existing DARTS algorithms.
The techniques of progressive pruning approach, grouping similar operations as well as a gradient confusion are promising to overcome the bottlenecks. 
The proposed method achieves promising performances on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet. 

Weakness:
The motivation of going for one-level optimization is not new. The original DARTS paper has ever studied the possibility of the one-level optimization while it may have some failures. Besides, there exist one work [a] sharing the same motivation. So I am concerned that the paper seems to miss this important related work. 
[a] Stamoulis et al., Single-path NAS: Designing hardware-efficient convnets in less than 4 hours. 2019.

The used strategies are straightforward and heuristic. While they bring some good results, I cannot see significant technical and theoretical contributions. On the other side, such techniques can be used for two-level optimization. So it would be better if the paper can show some evaluations on the original two-level optimization using these strategies. 

The grouping strategy looks very greedy for the early search. It starts from the group selection based on representative instances like 3*3 separable convolutions, 3*3 max pooling and 3*3 dilated convolution. If the 3*3 separable convolution is finally selected, it does not mean this kind of operations is optimal, because some other scaled operations like the 5*5 dilated convolution might be better than 3*3 dilated convolution.  

In section 3.2, the paper presents the correlation of the learned \alpha and the stand-alone model performance and I see a huge improvement of your method w.r.t. the origin DARTS (0.2 in DARTS and 0.91 in this paper). However, the evaluation method seems to be unclear to me and what do you mean by ‘replace the selected operation in the first edge of the first cell for the final architecture with all the other candidate operations in the first stage of StacNAS’’.

content.title: We thank the reviewer's comment and hope the following reply address the concerns.
content.comment:
The ablation study on each of the component proposed for both one-level and the original two-level optimization have been presented in Table 4. 

 The 'single-path NAS’ solves a problem with different scope from ours: they do not need to decide among identity, pooling or convolution, instead, this decision is made by the human-designed backbone. The problem they solved is to choose the kernel size of a convolution with a one-path search space. In the simpler search space, they argued one-level optimization was good enough. There was no claim that one level optimization would work well for multi-pass space of DARTS. Actually, it does not work well for the original DARTS: one would end up with a normal cell with all convolution operations for CIFAR10, CIFAR100 and IMAGENET. This is probably the reason that the DARTS paper used two-level optimization to prevent 'overfitting'. 


We believe that the contribution of this work is beyond proposing some techniques, we provide some deep understanding of the key points to get the DARTS systems to work: 1. Optimization complexity matching: we are the first to point out that using 8 cells during the search stage and 20 cells during final training make the system to select more than enough convolution, not the one-level optimization.  2. The use of a grouping strategy to prevent the system to break down under colinearity. DARTS works fine under the current search space but not an imbalanced one. 


 For the correlation map:  the purpose of the correlation map is to measure how the estimated alpha could represent the relative importance of the 7 candidate operations. To check this, we fix the rest of the best architecture and then change the first edge in the normal cell with all the 7 operations, and fully train them to obtain the 'true' accuracy of those 7 operations at this position.
